eras.title: Byzantion
eras.caption: A Greek colony from Megara on the point between the Golden Horn and the Bosporus, living off the grain ships out of the Black Sea and the tunny that crowd into its harbour. A modest walled town, its acropolis where Topkapı Palace now stands.

eras.title: New Rome
eras.caption: Constantine refounds the city as his capital in 330, with a forum, a hippodrome and a porphyry column bearing his statue. The land walls of Theodosius II (413) and the aqueduct of Valens close it in a ring of stone and water; an inventory of about 425 counts 4,388 great houses.

eras.title: The City of Justinian
eras.caption: Justinian's Hagia Sophia (537) lifts a dome that seems, Procopius writes, to hang from heaven by a golden chain. For six centuries this is the greatest city of Christendom, perhaps half a million people, its harbour closed in war by a chain across the Golden Horn.

captions.china: Tang records call it Fulin 拂菻, the city of the western king whose envoys reach Chang'an in 643. Du Huan, a prisoner taken at Talas, hears of its high walls and its skilled physicians.
captions.islam: To the caliphs it is al-Qustantiniyya, besieged by Arab fleets in 674–678 and again in 717–718 and never taken. Al-Mas'udi describes its walls, its harbour chain and the emperor's palace.

eras.title: The Shrunken Empire
eras.caption: Crusaders sack the city in 1204 and hold it for 57 years. The restored empire is a shadow: villages, orchards and ruins inside the walls, while Genoese Galata across the Golden Horn grows rich, crowned by its tower of 1348.

captions.islam: Ibn Battuta comes in 1332 in the train of a Byzantine princess married to the Uzbek khan, and describes the emperor's city on one side of the water and the Frankish merchants of Galata on the other.

eras.title: Ottoman Istanbul
eras.caption: Mehmed II takes the city in 1453. Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque and gains minarets; Topkapı Palace rises on the old acropolis among cypresses; Sinan's Süleymaniye (1557) crowns the third hill of the new Ottoman capital.

captions.europe: The city falls to the Ottomans in 1453, a shock across Latin Christendom. Europe's first printed views of it, like the Nuremberg Chronicle woodcut of 1493, are drawn largely from hearsay.

eras.title: City of Minarets
eras.caption: The Blue Mosque (1616), with its six minarets, faces Hagia Sophia across the old Hippodrome. Evliya Çelebi, born here in 1611, walks every quarter and counts its mosques, baths and guilds; caïques by the thousand ferry people across the water.

eras.title: Steam and the Republic
eras.caption: Steamers, a pontoon bridge across the Golden Horn and, from 1888, the railway from Europe. In 1923 the Republic moves the capital to Ankara; from 1930 the city is officially Istanbul to everyone.

eras.title: Istanbul across Two Continents
eras.caption: The first bridge across the Bosporus (1973) joins Europe and Asia, and the city spreads along both shores to more than fifteen million people. The old peninsula keeps its skyline of domes and minarets.
